data.title: Bitcoin hits lowest since July as Fed hike talk and a Wall Street rout collide
data.description:
The rates message (like this: J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call ) is hitting the whole crypto complex, not just Bitcoin. Ether dropped below $1,800 and sentiment gauges sit at extremes. Spot ETF products traded lower with the underlying, and IBIT and FBTC each fell less than 1% on the day. That leaves crypto equities such as COIN and MSTR, and listed miners, exposed to both falling token prices and a weaker tech tape. Bitcoin is trading as a high-beta risk asset rather than a hedge, so equity volatility and Fed pricing remain the main drivers for now.

---

data.title: 11-day Bitcoin redemption freeze: the risk hiding inside BTC-backed tokens
data.description:
At around 4,185 tokens, tBTC is far too small to move the BTC price, and the pause caused no visible spillover into spot Bitcoin, ETH or crypto equities. The pressure fell on DeFi lending. With redemption shut, liquidators taking tBTC collateral on Aave couldn’t fall back on redemption arbitrage, so they carried price and timing risk until they found a buyer. WBTC, cbBTC and other Bitcoin-backed tokens also depend on a bridge or custodian to keep minting and redemption open. Risk teams may now price that dependency into collateral settings more explicitly.

---

data.title: Euro breaks below $1.10 as French election risk builds; three banks see $1.08 next
data.description:
With short positioning this stretched, the euro is vulnerable to sharp short-covering rallies even if the trend stays lower. A credible French budget or a soft US inflation reading would be the likeliest triggers. On the downside, the $1.08 to $1.09 area is the next focus, where the bank forecasts and options-market risk sit. The spread between French and German bonds is the gauge to watch: if it stays contained, the move remains mainly a dollar story, and if it widens, the French element takes over. A firm dollar also keeps USD/JPY pressing against Tokyo’s intervention zone near 160.

---

data.title: Barclays: Back-to-back Fed hikes give the dollar staying power that a jumbo 50bp move wouldn’t
data.description:
The focus for the dollar shifts from how big the December hike will be to how long the hiking continues. That leans toward front-end Treasury yields staying high into the first quarter. It’s a constructive backdrop for the dollar against lower-yielding currencies, although intervention risk near 160 limits the upside in USD/JPY. Gold faces the same headwind it has struggled with all year, as longer-lasting high US rates raise the cost of holding it. Freight and diesel costs are a direct channel from oil to US core inflation, so oil prices now feed straight into Fed pricing.

---

data.title: Gold at $3,625: five forces behind the sell-off, and four reasons buyers haven’t quit
data.description:
Gold now trades below most major bank year-end targets, leaving it oversold on fundamentals but without a catalyst to turn it. With the $3,700 handle gone, traders are looking for support in the low $3,600s and high $3,500s, and a clean break would invite more momentum selling. The December 9 Fed decision is the main event risk: a 50 basis point hike or a higher dot plot would extend losses, while any hint the cycle is near its end could spark a sharp short-covering bounce. Miners are still far above record production costs, so margins can absorb further weakness, and supply is unlikely to tighten from producers cutting output.

---

data.title: J.P. Morgan now sees three straight Fed hikes, dropping its ‘December and done’ call
data.description:
A tier-one house moving from one more hike to three adds weight to the view that tightening doesn’t end in December, which supports two-year Treasury yields and the dollar. Pricing for 2027 is now where the action is, so January and March contracts are likely to firm. Strength against the yen is limited by a likely BoJ hike and intervention risk near 160. A Fed with no clear story to justify a pause makes every inflation release a market event, including any knock-on effects from oil.

---

data.title: Stock indices get beat up with the Dow, S&P, Nasdaq and Russell indices all falling more than 2%
data.description:
US stocks closed sharply lower Thursday, with all five major indices down more than 2%. The S&P 500 was up as much as 1.3% early before reversing to close down 2.02%, its sixth straight loss. The Dow shed 1,101 points, and only one of its 30 stocks finished higher.

Buyers had their shot early as demand for Anthropic lifted AI shares. That bid faded, and all seven Magnificent Seven stocks finished lower. Persistent inflation remains a headwind for valuations as investors weigh how long the Fed may need to keep policy tight. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 5.05% from 5.07% Wednesday, offering little relief for equities. investinglive.com

data.title: More from Fed’s Goolsbee: AI boom a ‘pig through the python’ that risks overheating US economy
data.description:
Goolsbee’s remarks add a demand-side argument to a Fed debate already leaning toward hikes. Markets heavily favour a quarter-point move on December 9, and a voice outside the usual hawks warning of overheating supports front-end yields and the dollar. He says inflation is not just an oil and tariff story, so a pullback in crude would ease less of the pressure than traders might hope. His uncertainty about how banks would cope with an AI-led equity correction marks a tail risk for stocks that could quickly reverse the tightening narrative.

---

data.title: Economic and event calendar in Asia Friday, November 20, 2026: Fed's Paulson, Japan CPI and China’s LPR
data.description: USD/JPY near 160 is where today’s events meet. A firm Japan CPI would support the yen at the margin, but a Fed that is also hiking limits how far the rate gap can narrow, and intervention warnings near 160 cap the upside. If Paulson sounds open to a 50 basis point move rather than gradual steps, front-end Treasury yields and the dollar would likely rise. Energy is a big part of Japan’s inflation pickup, so oil prices feed straight into the BoJ’s thinking. A hold on the LPR should barely move the yuan, while a surprise cut would stand out given the overnight-rate overhaul.

data.title: Fed’s Goolsbee says he sees no clear path back to 2% inflation
data.description:
Goolsbee’s comments on inflation, interest rates and AI investment crossed the wires.

  • What is happening with services inflation is important in understanding whether price pressures stem from demand or things like energy costs.
  • Inflation has proven to be far more persistent than was thought in 2025, and data center demand and AI-related wealth impact is adding to it.
  • The steepness of the interest-rate path will be rooted in whether “borderline disturbingly high” inflation is seen returning to Fed’s 2% target.
  • Does not see at this point that inflation is on the path back to 2%. It is not just coming from oil and tariff shocks, but a sizable demand component.
  • Is not concerned about wages pressuring inflation at this point.
  • It has not been good news on inflation for the past few months.
  • Anthropic’s IPO raises the question of how stockholders will use that wealth. It could have a macroeconomic impact.
  • Artificial intelligence is influencing today’s economy through wealth impacts and investment.
  • There is widespread acknowledgment among businesses that costs are up, particularly among firms in construction or competing with data centers for components.
  • Is not sure if fallout from US midterm elections will include a slowdown in data-center buildout or have a lasting impact on equity prices.
  • More openness about monetary policy has been productive for the Fed and the world.
  • Consumer spending has been pretty broad-based, financed mostly out of income growth.
  • There is a high risk that economy’s capacity cannot handle the current “pig-through-the-python” level of business investment without overheating.
  • Not clear how financial sector would be impacted if there is a major correction in equities related to AI.

data.title: AUDUSD moves to a new low.
data.description:
Australia’s October jobs report was considerably weaker than expected. Employment fell 43,500 against the 25,500 gain expected in our preview, and the unemployment rate rose to 4.9% versus 4.7% expected. September’s job loss was revised to 36,400 from 39,300, putting the two-month decline at nearly 80,000 jobs, the biggest in five years.

  • Full-time employment fell 2,900. Part-time employment fell 40,600.
  • Participation fell to 66.6% from 66.8%, while the number of unemployed people still rose by 17,800. Hours worked fell 0.2%.
  • Youth unemployment rose to 11.3% from 11.1%, also the highest since October 2021.

data.title: No relief for US stocks. Major indices trade to new lows
data.description:
US stocks are getting no relief. The Dow is down more than 1,000 points, the Nasdaq 100 is off more than 2%, and the Russell 2000 is down nearly 2%. The selling is broad, and the early lift from anticipation of Anthropic’s first trade has faded.

The concern for stocks is that persistent inflation could keep the Fed leaning toward tighter policy even as the risks to growth increase. Higher borrowing costs can weigh on spending and investment, while higher rates make it harder for investors to justify elevated valuations. That is a difficult combination for stocks, particularly when investors are already questioning how much growth they are willing to pay for.

data.title: Canada seeks interim U.S. tariff deal by year-end, CBC reports
data.description:
CBC News reported, citing sources familiar with Thursday’s meeting between Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and the federal government’s Canada-U.S. economic advisory committee, that Ottawa is aiming for an interim tariff agreement with the Trump administration. CBC News

  • Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada still wants a U.S. deal and is pursuing other trade opportunities. On his latest trip, Canada reached free trade deals with the Philippines and ASEAN and secured greater access to China for Canadian commodities.
  • Carney met with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China. The discussion ended without a trade breakthrough.
  • Carney told the DealBook Summit on Wednesday that talks had made progress in recent weeks, but the two sides had yet to put anything in writing.
  • Ottawa is seeking relief from Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber, along with Section 338 tariffs imposed on Canadian goods in August after earlier talks broke down.

data.title: Fed's Goolsbee: Job market is stable, but inflation is "way higher" than Fed's 2% target
data.description:
Comments from Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, a 2027 FOMC voter, crossed the wires on inflation, jobs and consumer demand.

  • The impact of tariffs has been more persistent than expected.
  • The job market is stable, but inflation is “way higher” than the Fed’s 2% target. Consumer demand has been very strong and solid.
  • AI seems promising as a boost to productivity but the day job of the Fed is to determine if the economy is overheating now
  • The job market is stable.
  • The Fed failure has been on inflation.
